newsitem.title: USA: With job cuts finished, Sunbeam focusing on growth.
newsitem.headline: With job cuts finished, Sunbeam focusing on growth.

text.p: With its drastic restructuring program now complete, appliance maker Sunbeam Corp. is looking forward to stronger sales in the second half of the year and possible acquisitions.

Company Chairman Albert Dunlap said the Delray Beach, Fla.-based company, which recently cut half of its 12,000 jobs and eliminated a large chunk of its product line, expects to introduce several new products to boost sales in the second half of the year and allow Sunbeam to double sales to $2 billion by 1999.

"The restructuring is now 100 percent behind us," Dunlap said in an interview Sunday. "We have sold all of the businesses we wanted to get out of. We're coming out with new products. We're now in the growth phase of the company.
"We're building up," he said. "The second half will be much stronger as the new products really begin to hit."
Dunlap said Sunbeam, best known for its Sunbeam and Oster appliances, was on target to double sales to $2 billion by 1999, with sales growth projected at 30 percent in 1998 and 35 percent in 1999.

Dunlap -- nicknamed "Chainsaw Al" and "Rambo in Pinstripes" for his corporate cost-cutting strategies -- shocked corporate America six months ago with plans to slash half of the struggling appliance maker's work force and eliminate 87 percent of its product lines.

The drastic measures -- announced four months after Dunlap became chairman -- were even more severe than Wall Street had expected, drawing fire from outgoing Labor Secretary Robert Reich, community activists and others.
"Every restructuring is extremely difficult," said Dunlap. "When you make those difficult decisions, you'll be criticized from every venue. That's the price you pay to be a leader."
But Dunlap -- who laid off more than 11,000 people at Scott Paper Co. before Kimberly-Clark Corp. acquired the company in late 1995 -- said his cost-cutting efforts at Sunbeam have already paid off.
Last week, the company reported 13 percent sales growth in the first quarter, its highest without the benefit of acquisitions since going public in 1992.
Sunbeam's success has fueled rumors the company may make an acquisition this year or put itself up for sale.
Dunlap declined to comment on his plans but he did not rule out an acquisition later this year.

"Any company that has as good a balance sheet as we're going to have, any company that's exhibiting the internal growth we're going to, and the profitability and the cash flow generation, certainly is always looking for the opportunity for acquisitions," Dunlap said. "Every opportunity that comes our way we'll take a look at."

Asked if he would consider the outright sale of Sunbeam -- founded in 1897 as Chicago Flexible Shaft -- Dunlap said, "Everything in the world is for sale at a great price." He would not elaborate further.
Dunlap said the company's focus for the time being would be on sales growth now that the company's restructuring and divestiture plan for non-core businesses has been completed.

"At this point in time, our major goal and objective is to generate profits, increase (market) share, increase sales and shareholder wealth," he said. "And as we go forward, we'll always consider every option available."
Sunbeam's stock dipped 12.5 cents to $31.125 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
